content.p: On the night of 3 November 1991, masked men with automatic weapons walked into a tenement courtyard at Jirón Huanta 840, in the Barrios Altos district of central Lima, where neighbours had gathered for a fund-raising meal. They ordered the guests onto the ground and opened fire. Fifteen people died, among them an eight-year-old boy, and four were seriously wounded. The attackers were soldiers and intelligence agents, members of a squad that became known as the Colina detachment, and they had come because military intelligence believed the building was used by the Shining Path guerrillas.

The victims were not guerrillas. A special chamber of Peru's Supreme Court said so in terms in 2009, when it convicted former president Alberto Fujimori over the killings. By then the case had produced a landmark ruling: in 2001 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held that the amnesty laws Peru had passed to protect the killers had no legal effect, and it later said that finding applied to every case in which those laws had been used. The story did not end with the verdicts: in December 2023 Fujimori was released from prison despite an instruction from that same court not to carry it out.
content.h2: A fund-raising meal in a crowded tenement
content.p: By 1991, the war between the Peruvian state and the Shining Path had moved into the capital. Peru's truth commission, in its account of the case, describes guerrilla car bombings and political murders in Lima that year, and a government that was preparing public opinion for a "hard hand" against the insurgency. Fujimori would shut down Congress and the courts in the self-coup of 5 April 1992.

The people at Jirón Huanta 840 were there for a "pollada", a type of neighbourhood event the Commission explains as a gathering held in the popular districts of Lima to cover an organiser's needs, in this case money for repairs to the property. The IEP timeline describes most of those present as street vendors and ice-cream sellers. Survivors told the Commission that between six and ten armed men in balaclavas, carrying submachine guns, burst into the patio and threatened about twenty guests. The Center for Justice and International Law counts six attackers. They insulted the guests, forced them face down, and fired bursts at heads and backs without distinction. Survivors and the forensic examinations agreed, the Commission records, that the dying were finished off with a shot at close range. Police collected 130 spent cartridge cases from the site.

Survivors' testimony places the attack at about 10:30 p.m., though one survivor quoted by the Commission put it at about ten, and the newspaper La República later reported 11:30 p.m. The Commission names all fifteen of the dead, aged from eight to 56. They included Manuel Isaías Ríos Pérez, 33, and his son Javier Ríos Rojas, 8, and the youngest adult was Benedicta Yanque Churo, 18. Four others survived with serious wounds, among them Tomás Livias Ortega.

Javier was the son of Manuel Isaías Ríos Pérez. A member of the unit who later cooperated with prosecutors under a protected identity told the court that the boy ran out to help his wounded father and was shot by one of the attackers, whom he named as Wilmer Yarlequé. A forensic ballistics report cited by the Commission counted eleven shots in the child's body. The same cooperating witness said the group quarrelled afterwards about the killing of the boy, and that Yarlequé answered that the chief had said no trace should remain.
content.h2: What the surveillance files and the witnesses say
content.p: The Commission's account draws on two former members of the detachment who gave statements to a Lima anti-corruption court in 2002 and 2003 under Peru's cooperation law. One said the squad's men had trained together and that other agents watched the building for hours beforehand, reporting to Major Santiago Martín Rivas, whom the witness named as the operation's head. The other described agents entering the tenement beforehand posing as guests and discovering that two separate gatherings were under way, one on each floor. According to the witness, an informant then went in to point out Shining Path members, and when asked who they were he answered "all of them". The shooting began after that. The witness said the squad arrived in two vehicles and afterwards went to a beach south of Lima, where Martín Rivas's birthday was being celebrated. These accounts come from the participants' own testimony and the Commission's summary of it; Martín Rivas has denied involvement, as set out below.

Documents in the public record supported the idea that the building had long been watched. Within days of the killings, senator Javier Diez Canseco showed the Senate's human rights commission two secret military intelligence notes. One described a surveillance operation, called Ambulante, on the property at Huanta 840 that had begun on 8 March 1989, on the theory that street-vendor leaders were meeting Shining Path commanders there. The ministers of the Interior and of Defense appearing before the commission offered three theories of authorship, the Shining Path, the Túpac Amaru movement, or other organisations, and flatly denied that the security forces had anything to do with it. The senators declared themselves unsatisfied and set up an investigating commission. Human Rights Watch notes that press reports soon after the killings also linked the attackers to the government and cited surveillance of the house.

The court reconstruction that took place in January 2002, after democracy returned, produced further findings recorded by the Commission. The attackers' retreat was covered by a troop-carrier carrying five uniformed army commandos. Police units posted very close by did not intervene. A judge established in 1995 that two utility vehicles described by witnesses belonged to the Interior Ministry and the Government Palace and had been reported stolen only days earlier. The tenement stood about 30 metres from the national police intelligence directorate, according to the Commission.

The Commission describes the killing as the first multiple homicide of civilians in the capital in that period of intensifying political violence, and the IEP timeline says that images of the bodies being carried out shook public opinion. The Senate's inquiry never finished. When Fujimori dissolved Congress in April 1992, papers disappeared, the Commission says, and on 24 April the prosecutor handling the case, Pablo Livia Torres, was dismissed without notice or a right to defend himself. Elected in November 1992, the new constituent Congress, where Fujimori's Cambio 90 held a majority, did not take the inquiry back up.

Journalists carried on instead. In 1992 the weekly Sí, edited by Ricardo Uceda, published evidence of a detachment called Colina linked to the intelligence services, and the Minister of Defense ordered a police investigation of the journalist, according to the Commission. Later that year and into 1993, Cecilia Valenzuela and Enrique Zileri of the magazine Caretas received death threats while looking into the case. On 1 April 1993 the congressman Henry Pease, citing an undisclosed source, said that an army intelligence special team had carried out the La Cantuta university killings of July 1992 and was also responsible for Barrios Altos. On 6 May 1993 General Rodolfo Robles, then among the army's most senior officers, made public a letter naming the Barrios Altos killings among the results of an operational command kept by army leaders. According to the Commission, he was expelled from the army the next day and, with his family, sought asylum in Argentina.

The state's own justice system moved only to bury the case. In September 1994 the military justice system secretly took the matter up, investigating generals and others including Montesinos, but only ordered that the accused appear and shelved it on 21 October 1994. It acted again in January 1995 under press pressure. In April 1995 a civilian prosecutor filed a complaint against the intelligence chief General Julio Salazar Monroe, Major Martín Rivas and three others, and a judge, Antonia Saquicuray, opened the case. Soldiers named in it refused to testify, and on 28 April the military's Supreme Council asked the Supreme Court to hand the case to military jurisdiction. Sources differ on the day the civilian investigation began: the Commission gives 18 April 1995 for the judge's order opening it, IDEHPUCP gives 15 April, and CEJIL gives 19 April.

The jurisdiction fight was not decided when Congress acted. In the early hours of 14 June 1995, the government majority passed Law 26479, which granted a general amnesty to military, police and civilian personnel for acts connected to the fight against terrorism since May 1980. The Commission quotes a source that puts the vote at 47 to 11. Opinion surveys the Commission cites found 87 per cent of respondents opposed.

Saquicuray refused to apply it. On 16 June she ruled that the amnesty could not cover the Barrios Altos case, writing that the American Convention obliges states to investigate human rights violations and punish those responsible. Congress answered with Law 26492, approved at once and without public debate on 29 June and published on 2 July. It declared the amnesty mandatory for the courts and not open to review by judges. A Lima appeals chamber then reversed Saquicuray on 14 July 1995, ordered the case closed for good and, according to the court judgment the Commission quotes, ordered her investigated for her reading of the law. A later appeal by the victims' relatives to the Supreme Court was thrown out. The second law became known as the Barrios Altos law.

The effect, in the Commission's words, was that people named in the Barrios Altos case, some still detained, benefited from the amnesty. On 30 June 1995, the day after Law 26492 was passed, a Peruvian human rights coalition, the Coordinadora Nacional de Derechos Humanos, lodged a complaint against Peru with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The Inter-American Commission issued its report on the case in March 2000. Fujimori left office in November 2000, and in 2001 the government of Valentín Paniagua took a different course. Peru acknowledged its international responsibility in a filing of 19 February 2001 and at the hearing on 14 March, accepting that it had breached the rights to life and personal integrity.

That same day the Inter-American Court of Human Rights gave judgment in Barrios Altos v. Peru. It held unanimously that the two amnesty laws were incompatible with the American Convention and "lack legal effect", and that Peru had to investigate and identify those responsible. In a later interpretation, dated 3 September 2001, the Court said the ruling had general effects, so that it applied to all the cases in which the two laws had been used, not only this one. CEJIL says the judgment set a precedent against impunity across the Americas.

The Court approved an agreement on reparations on 30 November 2001. Peru was to pay US$175,000 to each of the four survivors and to the beneficiaries of each person killed, except for the beneficiaries of Máximo León León, who were to receive US$250,000. It was also to provide free health care, study grants and educational materials, publish the judgment, build a memorial, and begin the process of ratifying the international convention on the non-applicability of statutory limitations to crimes against humanity. The Commission reported that the compensation had been paid. IDEHPUCP wrote in 2020 that most victims had received the money but that the memorial had not been built and that extrajudicial execution had not been made a criminal offence in Peru's code. It added that denialist comments about the victims persisted in Peruvian society.

At home, the courts began to undo the closure in 2001. According to the Commission, a Lima criminal chamber annulled the 1995 filing order, the prosecutors widened their complaint to Montesinos, Hermoza Ríos and thirteen others, and on 4 June 2001 the Supreme Council of Military Justice annulled its own earlier dismissals in favour of the generals, Montesinos and fifteen others. Human Rights Watch recorded that, after Congress lifted his immunity, the attorney general formally accused Fujimori of murder, causing grave injuries and disappearances, and that on 13 September 2001 a Supreme Court justice issued an arrest warrant through Interpol while he was living in Japan.

Human Rights Watch, in a 2005 analysis, argued that army intelligence documents referring to the "Destacamento Colina" showed it was an integral part of the military intelligence structure, with members assigned and disciplined by senior intelligence officers, and that former members said they operated from the National Intelligence Service's offices in 1991 and met Montesinos there. It also reported that Martín Rivas, in television interviews in 2003, said Fujimori had ordered a counter-subversion policy that he, Martín Rivas, had drafted, and later retracted those statements, claiming the recordings were fabricated, and went on to deny that Colina existed.

On 7 April 2009, a special chamber of the Supreme Court sentenced Fujimori to 25 years for the Barrios Altos and La Cantuta killings and two kidnappings, finding him the indirect author of aggravated murder, serious injuries and aggravated kidnapping. Amnesty International says the verdict was unanimous and that the sentence was the maximum under the code in force when the crimes were committed. The court described the killings as crimes against humanity. IDEHPUCP records that the Supreme Court's transitional criminal chamber upheld the judgment in full on 3 January 2010. Sources disagree on the year: CEJIL's blog says 2007, while Amnesty International, CNN, Human Rights Watch, Infobae and the Inter-American Commission say 2009.

The judgment also addressed the victims' reputations. El Comercio reported on the day of the verdict that the chamber said no investigation had found any indication that those who died, or the four survivors, were linked to the Shining Path. Gisela Ortiz, speaking for the families, said she was satisfied and that it was the first time a judgment cleared their relatives' names. Fujimorista congresswoman Cecilia Chacón said the chamber had gone beyond its role in declaring the victims innocent, though she added she could not say whether they were terrorists.

The IDEHPUCP argued in 2018 that a question was left open about the Colina detachment's aims. According to that article, the prosecutor's main argument was that the unit was created as part of an unofficial, illegal strategy approved by the government, and the Supreme Court's judgment developed only that thesis, not the political aims the prosecutor also mentioned. In his closing argument, Fujimori's lawyer César Nakasaki called any link between the unit and the 1995 election absurd. The IEP timeline quotes Martín Rivas as saying that the Barrios Altos operation was not meant to capture terrorists but to send a forceful message to the Shining Path.

On 1 October 2010, a separate chamber sentenced the chain of command and the squad's members. La República reports that Montesinos, Hermoza Ríos and other Colina members received 25 years. IDEHPUCP's summary of the proceedings lists sentences of between four and 25 years for the accumulated Barrios Altos, Santa and Pedro Yauri case, with Salazar Monroe, Martín Rivas, Pichilingue Guevara, Rivero Lazo and the others named among the convicted. In 2013, La República notes, Fujimori said he felt no pangs of conscience over the killings. In 2021, members of the Colina group asked for house arrest, and the request was refused.

On 24 December 2017, President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski granted Fujimori, in the words of the resolution Amnesty International quotes, "a pardon and the right to grace on humanitarian grounds". His office said Fujimori suffered from a progressive, degenerative and incurable disease. CEJIL's analysis said the decision came days after Kuczynski was saved from removal by ten votes from allies of Fujimori's son Kenji, and that it resonated as a corrupt political bargain. Human Rights Watch said it appeared to be a political manoeuvre. Outrage led to two nights of protests in Lima, according to CNN.

Victims' lawyers took the pardon to the Inter-American Court, which, CEJIL reported, would hold a hearing in Costa Rica on 2 February 2018. On 15 June 2018, Amnesty International reported, the Court ruled that Peru's courts must review whether the pardon unnecessarily and disproportionately affected the victims' access to justice. Human Rights Watch dates a related order to May 2018 and says the court found "serious questions" about the pardon's medical and legal basis. In October 2018 a Peruvian court found grave irregularities in the pardon, and the Supreme Court confirmed that, and Fujimori was back in prison by January 2019, Human Rights Watch says.

The Constitutional Tribunal overturned those rulings in March 2022 and ordered him freed; the Inter-American Court instructed Peru the following month not to implement that order, and he remained behind bars. On 4 December 2023 the Tribunal ordered his release again, saying the court's monitoring orders were not binding. Human Rights Watch reported that three justices signed the ruling, that there was one dissent, and that two other members said they were not asked to take part. The Inter-American Court repeated its instruction on 5 December, and Fujimori walked out of prison on 6 December. Human Rights Watch said the release violated Peru's international obligations; the Inter-American Commission also rejected the decision.
Alberto Fujimori died on 11 September 2024, aged 86, his daughter Keiko Fujimori announced; his oncologist said he had tongue cancer.
